goals: Understand how optimization and regularization affect singular-value spectra and the effective rank of weight matrices.
Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.
Understand the geometry and practical language-model fine-tuning behavior of LoRA and other low-rank updates.
Evaluate tradeoffs among model quality, memory, throughput, and communication cost across model scales.
Build an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.11730.question: In the LLaMA 124M–500M experiments, how were spectral weight decay and standard weight decay matched for validation loss, training compute, and SVD-LLM compression settings? Report the exact compression, distortion, and inference-speed comparisons and any stated limitations.

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. passages.text: Subspace Momentum SGD with Residual Correction (SMRC). Inspired by Chen et al. (2025a) , we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains optimizer states in a low-dimensional subspace and adds the residual gradient in its orthogonal complement to the update. We incorporate this framework into momentum SGD ( Liu et al., 2020 ) and propose SMRC, which keeps momentum only in the projected space and reduces optimizer-state memory from O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) to O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . Although the projected momentum update and the residual correction lie in orthogonal subspaces, they remain coupled across iterations. To overcome this difficulty, we devise a subspace virtual iterate strategy that absorbs the momentum into an auxiliary trajectory. SMRC achieves an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate for any fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Furthermore, since the dominant gradient subspace evolves during training, practical methods periodically refresh the projection matrix P P , and we accordingly extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant. A direct application of the single-stage analysis results in a mismatch between virtual iterates at stage boundaries. We design a boundary correction approach that preserves the consistency of the virtual sequence. Our multi-stage SMRC attains the same rate as that of single-stage SMRC.

Projected Muon with Residual Correction (PMRC). Beyond momentum SGD, we apply the residual correction framework to Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , an effective optimizer for LLM training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , and develop PMRC. It maintains momentum in the projected coordinates and applies the matrix sign to the low-dimensional momentum. This nonlinear dependence of the update on the momentum invalidates the subspace virtual-iterate construction used for SMRC. To address this challenge, we present a weighted momentum tracking analysis that jointly characterizes momentum accumulation and effects induced by the residual correction. The matrix-sign step corresponds to steepest descent under the spectral norm and is characterized by the nuclear norm ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) , whereas the residual gradient correction is measured in the Frobenius norm. We establish convergence under a mixed stationarity measure and PMRC attains the same O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) rate as that of full-space Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . Similarly, we generalize PMRC to a multi-stage setting with periodically refreshed projection bases that better capture the evolving dominant gradient subspace and improve practical performance. The multi-stage variant retains the same O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate.

Finally, we evaluate our methods through extensive experiments. On synthetic problems, we examine the residual correction and the multi-stage basis refresh in SMRC, and the results show that the residual correction restores convergence while periodic refreshes track the evolving dominant gradient subspace. For practical LLM training, we develop a practical implementation of PMRC and evaluate it on LLaMA pretraining across four model scales from 60 60 M to 1.3 1.3 B parameters and on six supervised finetuning settings. Our PMRC consistently performs favorably against prior memory-efficient methods across different model scales and training settings.

In this section, we provide the omitted details of the LLM supervised finetuning (SFT) experiments. For the instruction-following task, we train on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU and adopt a device micro-batch size of 16 16 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for Muon, GaLore, GoLore, GUM, and PMRC, and a device micro-batch size of 8 8 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is 128 128 in both cases. For the mathematical reasoning task, we train on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs and adopt a device micro-batch size of 4 4 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for the same methods and a device micro-batch size of 2 2 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is again 128 128 . For AdamW-based methods, we use the standard coefficients β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 and β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 . For Muon-based methods, the momentum coefficient is set to 1 − β = 0.95 1-\beta=0.95 with Nesterov momentum enabled. The matrix sign is approximated using 5 5 Newton–Schulz iterations, while one-dimensional parameters and embedding layers are optimized with AdamW.

Hyperparameter Tuning. For each model and optimization method we select the learning rate by a grid search over { 1 × 10 − 5 , 2 × 10 − 5 , 4 × 10 − 5 , 8 × 10 − 5 } \{1\times 10^{-5},2\times 10^{-5},4\times 10^{-5},8\times 10^{-5}\} for the instruction-following task and { 8 × 10 − 6 , 1 × 10 − 5 , 3 × 10 − 5 , 5 × 10 − 5 , 7 × 10 − 5 } \{8\times 10^{-6},1\times 10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5},7\times 10^{-5}\} for the mathematical-reasoning task. PMRC uses a residual cap at a ratio of 4 4 and we grid search γ ∈ { 2000 , 4000 , 8000 , 16000 } \gamma\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000\} . We select the parameters that achieve the highest accuracy on benchmarks. Additional results. We present the prompt-level and instruction-level strict accuracy on the IFEval benchmark in Table 9 . For completeness, we include the results of GUM with rank r = 256 r=256 , in addition to the memory-matched setting with r = 128 r=128 used in the main experiments. PMRC outperforms GUM at both ranks on all three models in both metrics. Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and alignment assumptions are required for the singular-mode birth, saturation, and decay results for GD, SignGD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC? Which empirical models or tasks test these predictions, and what limitations do the authors state?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

passages.section: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 .
passages.text: Fig. 2 compares quantities measured from the trajectories with the theoretical predictions. For birth, GD retains exponent p p , ideal Muon follows q q , instantaneous Adam interpolates between the Euclidean and normalized regimes, cumulative Shampoo moves from p p toward its history-adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 , and undamped K-FAC removes the singular-magnitude dependence with α b = 0 \alpha_{\mathrm{b}}=0 . The decay curves distinguish finite extinction under ideal Muon, exponential decay under undamped K-FAC, and the polynomial tails of GD and cumulative Shampoo. The saturation experiment further reveals optimizer-dependent mode ordering: GD and Adam converge faster for larger targets; undamped K-FAC is approximately target independent while Muon shows dependence; history-dominated Shampoo reverses the GD ordering. Thus the optimizers change relative spectral progress rather than merely rescaling a common trajectory. Figure 2: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 at depth L = 4 L=4 . (a) The birth exponent α b \alpha_{\mathrm{b}} separates Euclidean, normalized, history adapted, and curvature corrected dynamics. (b) The decay exponent α d \alpha_{\mathrm{d}} distinguishes finite extinction of Muon ( α d = q < 1 \alpha_{\mathrm{d}}\!=\!q\!<\!1 ) from the other optimizers. (c) The saturation coefficient β \beta reveals target dependent mode ordering. (a) Adam ϵ \epsilon controls the regime (b) Two phases of Shampoo (c) K-FAC λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}\!>\!0 restores barrier Figure 3: Optimizer state parameters control the local birth regime. Adam’s stability parameter ϵ \epsilon shifts the GD-to-SignGD crossover; Shampoo damping delays the transition from p p to p − 1 p-1 ; and K-FAC damping restores the GD exponent below its curvature threshold.

Fig. 8 studies the decay exponent of unsupported modes and focuses on Shampoo saturation, where mode order reversal can happen theoretically. For decay, increasing depth changes the small mode geometry through p = 2 − 2 / L p=2-2/L . Empirically, GD, Adam, and cumulative Shampoo follow the predicted increase α d = p + 1 = 3 − 2 L , \alpha_{d}=p+1=3-\frac{2}{L}, so deeper factorizations produce a steeper polynomial tail near zero. In contrast, undamped K-FAC remains close to α d = 1 \alpha_{d}=1 , reflecting its exponential decay law, while Muon exhibits a much weaker depth dependence, consistent with its normalized geometry. Thus depth does not affect all optimizers uniformly: it strengthens the Euclidean style barrier for GD like methods, but has much less impact on normalized or curvature corrected decay. For saturation, we focus on cumulative Shampoo because it is the optimizer for which mode reversal can happen and depth also affects it. Its asymptotic saturation coefficient depends on both target size and accumulated history, β Sh ​ ( μ ) = L ​ μ p D ⋆ ​ ( μ ) . \beta_{\rm Sh}(\mu)=\dfrac{L\mu^{p}}{D_{\star}(\mu)}. As a result, the ordering of saturation rates across target modes need not agree with GD. The right panel shows precisely this effect. For L = 2 L=2 , β \beta decreases with μ \mu , so smaller target modes saturate faster than larger ones. For L = 8 L=8 , the trend reverses and larger target modes saturate faster. The case L = 4 L=4 lies near the transition and becomes weakly nonmonotone. This depth driven change in ordering is the clearest empirical instance of the Shampoo mode reversal predicted by the theory.

Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. For multi-head attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , the same principle becomes sharper because attention introduces additional invariances: row-wise softmax is unchanged by additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and the frozen output projection. Table 1: Comparison with the closest related theoretical analyses of LoRA. This work Jang et al. (2024) Kim et al. (2025) Requires NTK linearization No Yes No Multilayer multi-head attention bound Yes (Thm. 4.4 ) No No Spurious local minima excluded No (Prop. 4.9 ) Yes (NTK) Partial Additional loss assumptions Differentiability and stagewise C 1 C^{1} regularity NTK-regime conditions Restricted strong convexity and smoothness Generalization bounds Yes Yes No Our contribution is summarized as follows.

• Low-rank representer theorem for trace-norm fine-tuning. For a frozen network in which an adapted block T T is observed only through a finite-rank linear map Φ ⁡ ( T ) \Phi(T) of bottleneck rank d Φ d_{\Phi} , we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\Phi} ; see Theorem 4.1 . The multi-stage extension is Theorem 4.3 . • Rank bounds from attention invariances. For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. Combining these invariances with projector compression gives the optimizer-dependent subspace rank bounds in Theorem 4.4 . • Generic first-order rank deficiency for factorized LoRA. For the weight-decayed LoRA factorization, we prove that after a generic positive semidefinite perturbation, full-column-rank first-order stationary points are excluded whenever the Pataki–Barvinok rank threshold exceeds the dimension of the associated family of symmetric KKT matrices; see Theorem 4.7 . The multistage and attention consequence are Theorem C.9 and Corollary 4.8 . This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation. • Perturbation transfer and generalization. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .

Using K out K_{\mathrm{out}} for the number of output coordinates in the linearized training predictions, their low-rank existence theorem gives a solution satisfying r ⁡ ( r + 1 ) 2 ≤ K out ​ N \frac{r(r+1)}{2}\leq K_{\mathrm{out}}N . Thus the rank scale in that analysis is r = ⌊ 8 ​ K out ​ N + 1 − 1 2 ⌋ r=\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{8K_{\mathrm{out}}N+1}-1}{2}\rfloor , or r = O ⁡ ( K out ​ N ) r=O(\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{out}}N}) in the scalar-output convention. Our results improve this comparison in two ways. First, our bottleneck reduction is exact for frozen upstream computation and does not linearize the network around the pretrained weights. Second, the optimizer’s rank scale is r ≤ min ⁡ { K out , N } r\leq\min\{K_{\mathrm{out}},N\} in Attention, and this is better than Jang et al. (2024) ’s bound. Afzal et al. (2025) also analyzed fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model and quantified when nonlinear fine-tuning stays close to the linearized problem. In contrast, our reduction is exact once upstream computation is frozen; no approximation-by-linearization argument is needed.

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .
We compare ResQAdam with AdamW in from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning, in terms of training loss, final perplexity and accuracy, and optimizer-state memory.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 3: Comparison of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput across different models. Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

We compare ResQAdam with AdamW in from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning, in terms of training loss, final perplexity and accuracy, and optimizer-state memory.

Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

For the most restrictive budgets, particularly K / N = 0.1 K/N=0.1 and 0.2 0.2 , the accuracy of the unpruned model also decreases slightly, indicating a tradeoff between aggressive compressibility and performance before pruning.

passages.text: However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. ORCA achieves the lowest final loss at both 25 25 B and 50 50 B tokens for the 0.8 0.8 B model, showing that its gain persists as the token budget increases. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). Across these MoE experiments, ORCA reduces final validation loss by 0.020 0.020 – 0.025 0.025 relative to Muon.

To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . Following [ 26 , 16 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the CLIP ViT-B/32 [ 14 ] on the seven image classification datasets, such as Cars [ 23 ] , DTD [ 7 ] , EuroSAT [ 20 ] , GTSRB [ 49 ] , RESISC45 [ 6 ] , SUN397 [ 60 ] , and SVHN [ 37 ] . In these datasets, we measured the top-1 test accuracy. We tuned the learning rate over { 0.0001 , 0.0002 , … , 0.001 } \{0.0001,0.0002,\dots,0.001\} for each method on the validation set in each dataset separately. Because Zhang et al. [68] reported that ViT-base models heavily depend on the Adam-based optimizers, we here tested only the AdamW methods with preconditioning. For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query and value matrices of the attention layers in the vision model of CLIP ViT-B/32. We also fixed the rank to r = 16 r=16 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 16 16 , the batch size to 64 64 , the weight decay to zero, the dropout to 0.05 0.05 , and the train epoch to 5 5 with a linear learning-rate schedule. Table 2 shows the results. We observed that our AdamW method achieves either the highest or second-highest top-1 test accuracy across datasets, leading to the highest average. These results validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning for LoRA on the image classification task.

Following [ 26 , 41 , 16 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the LLaMA2-7B [ 52 ] on the commonsense reasoning benchmark, which assesses the reasoning capabilities of the fine-tuned model across the eight datasets, such as BoolQ [ 8 ] , PIQA [ 5 ] , SIQA [ 48 ] , HellaS [ 62 ] , WinoG [ 47 ] , ARC-e [ 9 ] , ARC-c [ 9 ] , and OBQA [ 35 ] . In these datasets, we measured the top-1 test accuracy. For fair comparison, we first split a combined dataset of all train sets, i.e., Commonsense170K, into the train and validation sets, tuned the learning rate on the validation set, and then evaluated the fine-tuned model on the test set in each dataset. In this experiment, we tested the Adam methods with preconditioning. We tuned the learning rate over { 0.0001 , 0.0002 , … , 0.001 } \{0.0001,0.0002,\dots,0.001\} for each method on the validation set, similar to Sec. 7.3 . For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query, key, and value projections of the attention layers and the up and down projections of the feed-forward layers. We also fixed the rank to r = 32 r=32 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 64 64 , the batch size to 16 16 , the weight decay to zero, the dropout to 0.05 0.05 , and the train epoch to 3 3 with a linear learning-rate schedule. Table 3 shows the results. We observed that our AdamW method achieves either the highest or second-highest top-1 test accuracy across datasets, leading to the highest average. These results validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning for LoRA on the commonsense reasoning task.

To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 . inspect:2610.02202.question: How were agentic search and embedding retrieval compared on ScholarCatalyst? Specify the candidate corpus, author relevance judgments, retrieval budgets, Recall@20 results, and any stated evaluation limitations.

passages.text: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs.

Contact: {sohyeon,yoonho}@stanford.edu Project Page ohmyksh.github.io/project/ScholarCatalyst Dataset huggingface.co/ScholarCatalyst Code github.com/stanford-iris-lab/ScholarCatalyst Contributors ⧫ {\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\blacklozenge} Full list in Appendix Figure 1: ScholarCatalyst asks whether a system can retrieve prior papers that inspire progress on a research project. Such a paper may share little semantic similarity with the question yet offer an insight that advances the project ( right ), while topically related work may not ( left ).

All systems struggle to retrieve catalyst papers. Current retrievers miss most of the papers that inspired a project ( Table 3 ). General-purpose dense retrievers perform best, yet place 39% of author-identified inspiration papers in the top 20 for CoreQ and 51% for SubQ . Scientific-document retrievers (SPECTER2, OpenScholar) trail the general-purpose models by at least 16 points on CoreQ and 27 points on SubQ at Recall@20. BM25 and LateOn trail by 15–16 points on CoreQ and 18–25 points on SubQ . Together, these results suggest that domain-specific training on citation signals does not by itself solve this task. Among the pre-cutoff systems in our main experiment, CoreQ is harder than SubQ , consistent with its longer queries and smaller, almost entirely cited positive sets ( Table 2 ). We show later that reranking with an oracle candidate pool recovers part of this gap ( Section 4.4 ). Agentic search does not improve over embedding retrieval. We compare LLM search agents built on pre-cutoff models (GPT-4.1 and o3) against the strongest embedding model ( Table 3 ). Grep-based search, despite its recent success as a lightweight alternative to embedding retrieval ( Li et al., 2026 ; Sen et al., 2026 ) , performs substantially worse. It finds only 8% of gold query–paper pairs during search, compared with 46% for the tool-calling agent ( Figure 6 ).

We attribute this gap to candidate coverage , since regardless of how a model reasons, an agent can interact with the corpus only through its search queries. As the corpus scales, this constraint becomes more important because an agent can inspect only a small fraction of the corpus. Consistent with this account, agent recall rises with backbone capability yet remains close to the embedding retriever’s even for the strongest model ( Figure 6 ). If coverage is the limiting factor, progress will require embedding retrievers that surface inspiration papers in the first place and agents that build on those results to guide further exploration. We report Fable 5.1 separately because it falls outside our knowledge cutoff, and we analyze its results, together with agent failure cases and retrieval rationales, in Sections D.3 and D.6 .

We introduced ScholarCatalyst , a benchmark for one ingredient of research ability: identifying prior papers whose ideas could help a project move forward. Drawing on 184 researchers’ own accounts of what shaped their work, we capture judgments that the published record largely omits. Current systems recover only a fraction of the papers that authors credit, and agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval, largely because limited candidate coverage keeps many useful papers out of reach. Limitations. ScholarCatalyst covers computer science papers from 2025–2026 with uneven representation across research areas (Table 8 ), so our findings may not transfer to other fields. Our labels are retrospective judgments by paper authors and are thus subject to hindsight. A more fundamental open question is the skyline, i.e., the performance ceiling of this task. As a point of reference, the human reference accuracy on ImageNet (94.9% top-5 ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) ) was later exceeded, and reannotation studies found that subsequent gains increasingly reflected the idiosyncrasies of the original labels ( Beyer et al., 2020 ; Shankar et al., 2020 ) . Catalyst paper retrieval is harder to audit this way, since relabeling by anyone other than the authors would be costly and would measure a different target, namely what an informed outsider can infer. Still, a preliminary comparison on one paper with three author-annotators in ScholarCatalyst found that coauthors marking only about seven positives per thread recovered 43–60% of the first author’s labels at 84–88% precision. This is well above the best system’s overall R@5 of 0.24, which suggests considerable room for improvement.

Outlook. Recent work on reasoning-intensive retrieval evaluates relevance relations that require reasoning to recognize ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Tchuindjo et al., 2026 ) . What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs.

Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Quality runs train a 257M dense reference and a 1B MoE reference on FineWeb-Edu ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) . Systems benchmarks cover dense reference sizes up to 6.89B on an H100. These benchmarks measure the cost of the training operations at larger widths, while the complete pretraining runs test learning quality. Appendix A gives the protocols.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. Full-step measurements capture this crossover, which optimizer-step timings alone would miss. Table 2 : Training costs on one H100 at microbatch 4, indexed by the dense reference model size. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at
